finding: The commercial-roof section has an exception: if the fire code official decides the roof is shaped like a Group R-3 roof (as a pitched shingle roof may be), the residential pathway and ridge-setback rules can be used instead.

finding: The commercial rules call for interior pathways at least every 150 ft, plus 4-ft straight-line pathways to standpipes or ventilation hatches and around roof access hatches.
source_title: Fire Marshal's Office – Solar Photovoltaic Power Systems (IFC 2021 Section 1205 text)
quote: Pathways shall be provided at intervals not greater than 150 feet (45 720 mm) throughout the length and width of the roof. A pathway not less than 4 feet (1219 mm) wide in a straight line to roof standpipes or ventilation hatches.

finding: Under the residential-type rules, at least two 36-inch pathways from the eave to the ridge are required, and the ridge setback is 18 in. on each side if the array covers 33% or less of the plan-view roof area, or 36 in. if it covers more.
value: 2 × 36 in pathways; ridge setback 18 in (≤33%) / 36 in (>33%)
source_title: Fire Marshal's Office – Solar Photovoltaic Power Systems (IFC 2021 Section 1205 text)
quote: 1205.2.1.2 Setbacks at ridge. For photovoltaic arrays occupying 33 percent or less of the plan view total roof area, a setback of not less than 18 inches (457 mm) wide is required on both sides of a horizontal ridge.

finding: Pathways must cross areas that can carry firefighters and must be kept as free as possible of obstructions such as vent pipes, conduit and equipment, so new skylight domes should be kept out of required pathways.
value: Pathways over load-bearing areas, minimal obstructions
source_title: Fire Marshal's Office – Solar Photovoltaic Power Systems (IFC 2021 Section 1205 text)
quote: Pathways shall be over areas capable of supporting fire fighters accessing the roof. Pathways shall be located in areas with minimal obstructions, such as vent pipes, conduit or mechanical equipment.

finding: The CAL FIRE commercial guideline (an April 2008 draft, which predates current code) treats skylights as reference points: pathways run in a straight line 4 ft wide to skylights, and a 4-ft pathway beside existing skylights is one accepted smoke-ventilation option between array sections.

finding: The Canadian Conservation Institute says visible light, not just UV, is what fades sensitive dyes; UV often causes less than half of the fading, so a UV-filtered skylight still fades rugs unless overall light exposure is limited.
value: UV usually <½ (often ~1/10) of fading for light-sensitive colours
source_title: Agent of deterioration: light, ultraviolet and infrared (Canadian Conservation Institute)
quote: For colours that are sensitive to light — the crux of the museum lighting dilemma — UV usually contributes less than half of the fading and often only one tenth

finding: CCI estimates that colours with high light sensitivity show a just-noticeable fade within about 1/7 to 2 years at office-level light (500 lux), and within 1 day to 2 weeks at average daylight levels.
source_title: Agent of deterioration: light, ultraviolet and infrared (Canadian Conservation Institute)
quote: 500 lux office | Just noticeable fade | 30 – 700 years | 2 – 70 years | 1/7 – 2 years

finding: The U.S. Department of the Interior museum standard caps light at 50 lux for light-sensitive materials such as dyed textiles and tapestries, and requires UV filtering when UV exceeds 75 microwatts per lumen.
source_title: Departmental Manual 411 DM 2 – Museum Property Management Standards (DOI)
quote: If the UV radiation level exceeds 75 microwatts per lumen, it is mandatory to control it by installing UV-filtering material between the light source and museum property.

finding: AMNH notes that light damage is cumulative and irreversible and depends on intensity times hours, so placing rugs away from the diffusers and limiting how long they are exposed both reduce fading.
value: Damage = lux × hours (e.g., 50 lux × 24 h = 200 lux × 6 h)
source_title: Light, Ultraviolet, and Infrared: Impact on Collections | AMNH
quote: Light damage, which is cumulative and irreversible, is a function of light intensity multiplied by the duration of exposure.
